idiom_name: generic algebra interface parameterised by a representation type (Sym[R any])
implementation_notes: Since Go 1.18 generics let the algebra be parameterised by the representation type (`type Sym[R any] interface { Lit(i int) R; Add(a, b R) R }`), which is the final encoding for a first-order DSL: interpreters are structs implementing Sym[int], Sym[string], Sym[Query], and the program is a generic function `func Exp[R any](s Sym[R]) R`. What is not expressible is the higher-kinded half: R is a proper type, not a type constructor, and Go forbids methods with their own type parameters, so an algebra whose result type varies per operation (a lambda form, several DSL types) or that abstracts over the effect monad has no encoding. There, fall back to a plain interpreter interface injected explicitly (dependency injection) or to code generation, and accept that the effect is fixed.
pitfalls: R is fixed per instantiation: to interpret into an effect you must make the effectful value itself the representation (`Sym[IO[int]]`), which pushes sequencing into the program and gives up the F-polymorphism the pattern is about.
No implicit resolution: the interpreter must be threaded through every function that needs it, so a program that forgets a parameter silently hard-codes the production interpreter.
Generic instantiation compiles a copy per type argument, so many interpreters inflate build time and binary size; keep the algebra small.
Interface methods on pointer versus value receivers decide whether interpreters are copied - a stateful interpreter with a value receiver silently loses its writes.
